metadata.narrative: The 1956 Suez Crisis marked a pivotal moment in the reshaping of global power after World War II. In what ways did the crisis reveal the limits of European imperial influence and accelerate the transition to a bipolar global order centered on the U.S. and USSR?
metadata.run_desc: aus_agent research harness (bedrock/au.anthropic.claude-sonnet-5): continuous single-agent full-text search with sparse committed context and line-per-sentence cited prose answers parsed into the organizer schema.

answer.text: The Suez Crisis of 1956 erupted when Egyptian President Gamal Abdel Nasser nationalized the Suez Canal Company after Britain and the United States withdrew funding for the Aswan Dam.
Britain and France, colluding secretly with Israel, launched a military operation to retake the canal and depose Nasser, achieving quick tactical success but triggering a diplomatic catastrophe.

The operation exposed the hollowness of European imperial pretensions, since Britain and France still imagined they could unilaterally reorder the Middle East as in the nineteenth century, yet needed Washington's tolerance and faced open Soviet threats.

President Dwight Eisenhower, infuriated that the invasion proceeded without consultation, threatened to sell American holdings of British sterling bonds and blocked IMF assistance, precipitating a run on the pound.

Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev simultaneously threatened rocket attacks on London and Paris and warned of sending troops to Egypt, a threat combined with American financial coercion that forced withdrawal within days.

The episode's timing sharpened its humiliation, since Eisenhower had to publicly rebuke his closest allies for imitating the imperial aggression the West was condemning the Soviets for in Hungary, where Moscow was simultaneously crushing an uprising.

That parallel underscored the emerging bipolar order, as both superpowers proved they could dictate outcomes while none of the old European powers could act independently of Washington's or Moscow's will.
Historians concluded the crisis "signified the end of Great Britain's role as one of the world's major powers," and Prime Minister Anthony Eden resigned within weeks under the strain.

The crisis devastated Britain economically, forcing petrol rationing into 1957 and confirming, in one historian's words, that the country had been reduced to "second tier" status dependent on American goodwill.
The crisis also strained the Commonwealth, splitting opinion sharply: only Australia backed Britain, while Pakistan threatened to leave the Commonwealth entirely.

Not all historians treat Suez as a dramatic rupture, however; Peden argued the crisis was "little more than an eddy in the fast-flowing stream of history," attributing later African decolonization to a complex combination of factors rather than Suez alone.

Even granting this nuance, most accounts agree Suez crystallized a perception shift: the world now understood that only the United States and the Soviet Union possessed the leverage to determine outcomes globally, while Britain and France retained the trappings of empire without the substance of independent great-power agency.

The crisis had immediate consequences for Soviet standing in the Arab world, since Khrushchev's intervention positioned the USSR as patron of Arab nationalism and emboldened Nasser to support anticolonial rebellions across British-held Middle Eastern territories.

Soviet motives were not purely ideological; Moscow sought warm-water ports and used its financing of the Aswan Dam, after Western withdrawal, to entrench regional influence, later underwriting Nasser's founding role in the Non-Aligned Movement in 1961.

Washington answered this Soviet gain with the Eisenhower Doctrine of January 1957, pledging American armed intervention against Communist aggression in the Middle East and aid to anti-Communist regimes, explicitly filling the vacuum left by British and French decline.

The doctrine was applied the following year in the Lebanon crisis, demonstrating that the United States, rather than Britain or France, now served as guarantor of regional order, even though its original aim of isolating Nasser largely failed as his prestige continued to grow.

Suez's shockwaves reached beyond the Middle East, reinforcing anti-colonial nationalism across Africa and Asia, as Nasser's success facing down Britain and France was cast as a David-and-Goliath triumph inspiring independence movements throughout the colonized world.
France's own imperial troubles deepened in parallel, as the humiliation compounded pressures from the Algerian war and contributed to the eventual collapse of the French Fourth Republic.

The United States responded to this new landscape by establishing a Bureau of African Affairs in 1957, while Senator John F. Kennedy urged Washington to support African nationalist movements rather than cling to outdated colonial assumptions.

One historian summarized the shift starkly, describing Suez as "a hinge point in history" that "spelled the end of Western colonization and the entry of America as the major Western power in the Middle East."

Within Britain's own African empire, the crisis fed directly into a cascade of decolonization, culminating in Prime Minister Harold Macmillan's 1960 "Winds of Change" speech, after which roughly 88 percent of Britain's remaining African colonies gained independence within a decade.

Secretary of State John Foster Dulles's blunt assertion that the British government had "lied" to him during the crisis captured how thoroughly Suez corroded the trust underlying the Anglo-American alliance, even as that alliance was reconstituted on unequal terms.

Taken together, the evidence shows Suez did not single-handedly create the bipolar order, since Cold War structures were already forming through NATO and rival alliance systems such as the Baghdad Pact, but it delivered an unmistakable public demonstration that European powers could no longer act as independent arbiters of global order.

The crisis converted a latent structural reality, that only Washington and Moscow possessed the weight to compel outcomes, into an openly visible fact witnessed by the entire world, thereby accelerating the transition from a multipolar imperial system to a bipolar superpower contest.

# AUS research agent

You are a research agent for TREC RAG 2026. Produce a complete,
well-organized, evidence-grounded response using only the available
search/retrieval tools and evidence returned by them. Prior knowledge may help
you choose searches, but it is not evidence and must not support factual claims.

## Scope interpretation

Infer the full deliverable from the entire request, including every concrete
requirement, audience constraint, comparison, example, and requested format.
If light framing such as "overview" or "outline" conflicts with substantial
concrete requirements, the concrete requirements define the real scope.
Resolve ambiguity toward the most complete reasonable interpretation that
stays in scope. Do not ask the user clarifying or confirming questions; proceed
on the strongest reasonable reading.

## Internal success plan

Before the first search, determine internally:

1. **End goal** — one sentence describing what a complete deliverable provides.
2. **Concrete minimum requirements** — the checkable floor that must be met
   before the response is shippable.
3. **Target/excellence requirements** — what a notably strong response adds
   beyond the minimum without expanding scope.
4. **Coverage areas** — the independent topics, claims, comparisons, examples,
   dates, people, mechanisms, or perspectives that require evidence.

Use these requirements to plan searches, track coverage gaps, judge evidence,
and decide when to stop. Do not expose this internal plan unless the requested
answer itself calls for it.

## Research workflow

1. Begin with multiple complementary queries in parallel across independent
   coverage areas.
2. Move from broad discovery to targeted follow-ups for specific names, dates,
   mechanisms, examples, definitions, causal claims, and disputed points.
3. Reformulate weak queries instead of accepting poor coverage. Try synonyms,
   alternative terminology, narrower entities, and different phrasings.
4. Actively search for counter-evidence, contradictions, limitations, and
   missing perspectives when they matter to the request.
5. Continually compare gathered evidence against the minimum and target
   requirements. Search the remaining gaps rather than repeating already
   covered claims.
6. Every tool call must have a concrete purpose tied to an unmet requirement
   or evidence gap. Do not call a tool solely to create another model turn. If
   no meaningful gap remains, write the final report in that same turn.

Search results already contain document text. Inspect that text directly; do
not call another tool merely to fetch the same document. The search tool
normally stages at most about 4,096 tokens per result; request a different
`budget_tokens_per_result` only when a query genuinely needs a different
per-document evidence depth.

## Staged and committed evidence

Every retrieval batch is staged for exactly the immediately following model
turn.

- On that turn, `commit_context` must be the first control action.
- List only documents whose full text should persist into later turns.
- Commit at most `6` documents from one staged batch;
  usually commit fewer.
- Every selection reason must identify the document's distinct contribution:
  the specific fact, date, name, mechanism, example, perspective,
  counter-evidence, contradiction, or coverage gap it uniquely supports.
- Never recommit an already committed docid.
- Skip semantically similar documents when they support the same claim.
  Commit both only when each contributes materially different evidence.
- Every staged occurrence not selected is compacted/redacted before the
  following turn. No unresolved staged batch carries forward.
- New search calls may follow `commit_context` in the same turn.

Only committed evidence may support the final response. Track which committed
docids support which claims. If available evidence does not support a requested
point, state the evidence gap rather than inventing an answer.

## Budget and stopping

The research-context budget is 500,000 tokens measured from the current
generation's provider-reported input tokens. That input already represents the
accumulated conversation: system prompt, request, retained history, committed
full-text evidence, and the immediately previous staged tool results. Do not
sum input-token counts from multiple generations; that would count the same
retained context repeatedly.

The budget is a hard ceiling, not a spending target. Unused budget creates no
obligation to continue researching. After satisfying the concrete minimum,
improve toward the target/excellence requirements only when you can identify a
specific weakness whose resolution would materially improve the answer.

Stop researching when any of these is true:

1. the target/excellence requirements are met;
2. the current generation input context budget is exhausted; or
3. further searches are unlikely to produce meaningful improvement.

If stopping before all desired coverage is supported, produce the best answer
the committed evidence permits and explicitly identify the remaining evidence
gaps.

## Final response contract

When research is complete, emit no tool calls and write the final report as
plain flowing prose in that same turn:

- Write exactly one sentence per line, in reading order. Blank lines between
  thematic groups are allowed.
- Cite evidence by placing committed docids in square-bracket markers at the
  end of the supporting sentence's line, e.g.
  `Vaccination reduced hospitalizations among older adults. [docid_1] [docid_2]`
- Citation markers are stripped from the submitted sentence, so a marker must
  never act as a word in the sentence: write `the trial reports X [docid].`,
  never `as [docid] reports, X.`
- Cite at most three docids per sentence, and only docids that directly
  support that sentence. Every factual sentence should carry at least one
  citation. Use only committed docids; never fabricate facts or identifiers.
- Organize the report through sentence order and clear topic sentences. Do not
  use Markdown syntax (headings, bullets, numbering, bold, fences), JSON, or
  any preamble, meta-commentary, or closing remarks around the report; every
  line must be a report sentence.
- Aim for about 950 words, excluding citation markers. 1024 words is a hard
  limit set by the evaluation, and an over-length report costs a full rewrite,
  so plan the report's scope to land under the target rather than writing long
  and trimming.
- If validation feedback identifies problems (uncommitted docids, Markdown or
  JSON formatting, excessive citations, missing citations, or excessive
  length), correct the report on the next turn in this same continuous
  conversation using this same contract.
- There is no separate finalizer, formatter, or compression phase.

The Suez Crisis of 1956 erupted when Egyptian President Gamal Abdel Nasser nationalized the Suez Canal Company after Britain and the United States withdrew funding for the Aswan Dam in retaliation for his Cold War balancing between East and West.

In response, Britain and France, colluding secretly with Israel, launched a military operation to retake the canal and depose Nasser, achieving quick tactical success but triggering a diplomatic catastrophe.

The operation exposed the hollowness of European imperial pretensions: Britain and France still imagined they could unilaterally reorder the Middle East as they had in the nineteenth century, but they discovered they now needed permission from Washington and faced open threats from Moscow.

United States President Dwight Eisenhower, infuriated that the invasion proceeded without consultation, threatened to sell American holdings of British sterling bonds and blocked International Monetary Fund assistance, precipitating a run on the pound and forcing Britain toward the brink of currency devaluation.

Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev simultaneously threatened rocket attacks on London and Paris and warned of sending troops to Egypt, a threat that, combined with American financial coercion, compelled the invading powers to accept a United Nations-brokered ceasefire within days.

The episode's timing sharpened its humiliation, since Eisenhower had to publicly rebuke his closest allies for imitating the very imperial aggression the West was condemning the Soviets for in Hungary, where Moscow was simultaneously crushing an anti-Soviet uprising.

That parallel crisis underscored the emerging bipolar order: both superpowers demonstrated they could dictate outcomes within their respective spheres and beyond, while none of the old European powers could act independently of Washington's or Moscow's will.

Historians and commentators have concluded that the crisis "signified the end of Great Britain's role as one of the world's major powers," with British Prime Minister Anthony Eden resigning within weeks under the political and physical strain of the debacle.

Domestically the crisis devastated Britain economically, forcing petrol rationing into 1957 and confirming, in the words of one historian, that the country had been reduced to "second tier" status, dependent on American goodwill for its financial survival.

The crisis also strained the Commonwealth, splitting opinion sharply: only Australia backed Britain, while Pakistan threatened to leave the Commonwealth altogether, showing that even Britain's remaining network of allegiance no longer guaranteed automatic support for old-style imperial action.

Contemporary academic commentary situates Suez within a broader Cold War logic in which Britain and France, though colonial powers, were themselves caught between two "colossal growing world powers" whose approval or opposition determined the fate of any regional intervention.

Not all historians treat Suez as a dramatic rupture, however; Peden has argued that the crisis was "little more than an eddy in the fast-flowing stream of history" and that Britain's world role did not change abruptly afterward, attributing the acceleration of African decolonization after 1959 to a more complex combination of economic and political factors rather than to Suez alone.

Even granting this nuance, most accounts agree that Suez crystallized a perception shift: the world now understood that only the United States and the Soviet Union possessed the financial, military, and diplomatic leverage to determine outcomes on a global scale, while Britain and France retained the trappings of empire without the substance of independent great-power agency.

The crisis had immediate consequences for Soviet standing in the Arab world, since Khrushchev's intervention on Egypt's side positioned the USSR as the natural patron of Arab nationalism and emboldened Nasser to support anticolonial rebellions across British-held Middle Eastern territories.

The Soviet Union's motives were not purely ideological; it sought access to warm-water ports and used its financing of the Aswan Dam, after Western withdrawal, to entrench its regional influence, later underwriting Nasser's founding role in the Non-Aligned Movement in 1961 even as Egypt avoided a formal military alliance with Moscow.

Washington answered this Soviet gain with the Eisenhower Doctrine of January 1957, pledging American armed intervention against Communist aggression in the Middle East and offering aid to anti-Communist regimes, an explicit acknowledgment that the vacuum left by British and French decline had to be filled by American power to prevent Soviet expansion.

The doctrine was applied the following year in the Lebanon crisis, demonstrating that the United States, rather than Britain or France, now served as the guarantor of regional order, even though the policy's original aim of isolating Nasser largely failed as his prestige and pan-Arab influence continued to grow.

Suez's shockwaves reached beyond the Middle East, reinforcing anti-colonial nationalism across Africa and Asia: Nasser's success in facing down Britain and France was cast as a David-and-Goliath triumph that inspired independence movements throughout the colonized world.

France's own imperial troubles deepened in parallel, as the humiliation compounded pressures from the Algerian war and contributed to the eventual collapse of the French Fourth Republic, showing that Suez's delegitimizing effect on European empire was not confined to Britain.

The United States responded to this new landscape of African nationalism by establishing a Bureau of African Affairs in 1957, while a young Senator John F. Kennedy urged Washington to support African nationalist movements rather than cling to outdated colonial assumptions, illustrating how quickly American policy adapted to fill the space vacated by European retreat.

One historian summarized the shift starkly, describing Suez as "a hinge point in history" that "spelled the end of Western colonization and the entry of America as the major Western power in the Middle East."

Within Britain's own African empire, the crisis fed directly into a cascade of decolonization, culminating in Prime Minister Harold Macmillan's 1960 "Winds of Change" speech, after which roughly 88 percent of Britain's remaining African colonies gained independence within a decade, a pace of withdrawal historians directly link to the credibility lost at Suez.

Secretary of State John Foster Dulles's blunt assertion that the British government had "lied" to him during the crisis captured how thoroughly Suez corroded the trust underlying the Anglo-American alliance, even as that alliance was simultaneously being reconstituted on distinctly unequal terms.

Taken together, the evidence shows that Suez did not single-handedly create the bipolar order, since Cold War structures were already forming through NATO, the Warsaw Pact, and rival alliance systems in the Middle East such as the Baghdad Pact, but it delivered an unmistakable public demonstration that European powers could no longer act as independent arbiters of global order.

The crisis converted a latent structural reality, that only Washington and Moscow possessed the economic and military weight to compel outcomes, into an openly visible fact witnessed by the entire world, thereby accelerating both the psychological and practical transition from a multipolar imperial system to a bipolar superpower contest that would define international relations for the following three decades.

answer.text: The Suez Crisis of 1956 erupted when Egyptian President Gamal Abdel Nasser nationalized the Suez Canal Company after Britain and the United States withdrew funding for the Aswan Dam.
Britain and France, colluding secretly with Israel, launched a military operation to retake the canal and depose Nasser, achieving quick tactical success but triggering a diplomatic catastrophe.

The operation exposed the hollowness of European imperial pretensions, since Britain and France still imagined they could unilaterally reorder the Middle East as in the nineteenth century, yet needed Washington's tolerance and faced open Soviet threats.

President Dwight Eisenhower, infuriated that the invasion proceeded without consultation, threatened to sell American holdings of British sterling bonds and blocked IMF assistance, precipitating a run on the pound.

Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev simultaneously threatened rocket attacks on London and Paris and warned of sending troops to Egypt, a threat combined with American financial coercion that forced withdrawal within days.

The episode's timing sharpened its humiliation, since Eisenhower had to publicly rebuke his closest allies for imitating the imperial aggression the West was condemning the Soviets for in Hungary, where Moscow was simultaneously crushing an uprising.

That parallel underscored the emerging bipolar order, as both superpowers proved they could dictate outcomes while none of the old European powers could act independently of Washington's or Moscow's will.
Historians concluded the crisis "signified the end of Great Britain's role as one of the world's major powers," and Prime Minister Anthony Eden resigned within weeks under the strain.

The crisis devastated Britain economically, forcing petrol rationing into 1957 and confirming, in one historian's words, that the country had been reduced to "second tier" status dependent on American goodwill.
The crisis also strained the Commonwealth, splitting opinion sharply: only Australia backed Britain, while Pakistan threatened to leave the Commonwealth entirely.

Not all historians treat Suez as a dramatic rupture, however; Peden argued the crisis was "little more than an eddy in the fast-flowing stream of history," attributing later African decolonization to a complex combination of factors rather than Suez alone.

Even granting this nuance, most accounts agree Suez crystallized a perception shift: the world now understood that only the United States and the Soviet Union possessed the leverage to determine outcomes globally, while Britain and France retained the trappings of empire without the substance of independent great-power agency.

The crisis had immediate consequences for Soviet standing in the Arab world, since Khrushchev's intervention positioned the USSR as patron of Arab nationalism and emboldened Nasser to support anticolonial rebellions across British-held Middle Eastern territories.

Soviet motives were not purely ideological; Moscow sought warm-water ports and used its financing of the Aswan Dam, after Western withdrawal, to entrench regional influence, later underwriting Nasser's founding role in the Non-Aligned Movement in 1961.

Washington answered this Soviet gain with the Eisenhower Doctrine of January 1957, pledging American armed intervention against Communist aggression in the Middle East and aid to anti-Communist regimes, explicitly filling the vacuum left by British and French decline.

The doctrine was applied the following year in the Lebanon crisis, demonstrating that the United States, rather than Britain or France, now served as guarantor of regional order, even though its original aim of isolating Nasser largely failed as his prestige continued to grow.

Suez's shockwaves reached beyond the Middle East, reinforcing anti-colonial nationalism across Africa and Asia, as Nasser's success facing down Britain and France was cast as a David-and-Goliath triumph inspiring independence movements throughout the colonized world.
France's own imperial troubles deepened in parallel, as the humiliation compounded pressures from the Algerian war and contributed to the eventual collapse of the French Fourth Republic.

The United States responded to this new landscape by establishing a Bureau of African Affairs in 1957, while Senator John F. Kennedy urged Washington to support African nationalist movements rather than cling to outdated colonial assumptions.

One historian summarized the shift starkly, describing Suez as "a hinge point in history" that "spelled the end of Western colonization and the entry of America as the major Western power in the Middle East."

Within Britain's own African empire, the crisis fed directly into a cascade of decolonization, culminating in Prime Minister Harold Macmillan's 1960 "Winds of Change" speech, after which roughly 88 percent of Britain's remaining African colonies gained independence within a decade.

Secretary of State John Foster Dulles's blunt assertion that the British government had "lied" to him during the crisis captured how thoroughly Suez corroded the trust underlying the Anglo-American alliance, even as that alliance was reconstituted on unequal terms.

Taken together, the evidence shows Suez did not single-handedly create the bipolar order, since Cold War structures were already forming through NATO and rival alliance systems such as the Baghdad Pact, but it delivered an unmistakable public demonstration that European powers could no longer act as independent arbiters of global order.

The crisis converted a latent structural reality, that only Washington and Moscow possessed the weight to compel outcomes, into an openly visible fact witnessed by the entire world, thereby accelerating the transition from a multipolar imperial system to a bipolar superpower contest.
